original_value: AbstractData processing is increasingly becoming the subject of various policies and regulations, such as the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) that came into effect in May 2018. One important aspect of GDPR is informed consent, which captures one’s permission for using one’s personal information for specific data processing purposes. Organizations must demonstrate that they comply with these policies. The fines that come with non-compliance are of such importance that it has driven research in facilitating compliance verification. The state-of-the-art primarily focuses on, for instance, the analysis of prescriptive models and posthoc analysis on logs to check whether data processing is compliant to GDPR. We argue that GDPR compliance can be facilitated by ensuring datasets used in processing activities are compliant with consent from the very start. The problem addressed in this paper is how we can generate datasets that comply with given consent “just-in-time”. We propose RDF and OWL ontologies to represent the consent that an organization has collected and its relationship with data processing purposes. We use this ontology to annotate schemas, allowing us to generate declarative mappings that transform (relational) data into RDF driven by the annotations. We furthermore demonstrate how we can create compliant datasets by altering the results of the mapping. The use of RDF and OWL allows us to implement the entire process in a declarative manner using SPARQL. We have integrated all components in a service that furthermore captures provenance information for each step, further contributing to the transparency that is needed towards facilitating compliance verification. We demonstrate the approach with a synthetic dataset simulating users (re-)giving, withdrawing, and rejecting their consent on data processing purposes of systems. In summary, it is argued that the approach facilitates transparency and compliance verification from the start, reducing the need for posthoc compliance analysis common in the state-of-the-art.

result.paraphrase: AbstractData processing is increasingly governed by policies and regulations, including the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which took effect in May 2018. A key element of GDPR is informed consent, meaning permission to use personal information for specific data-processing purposes. Organizations must be able to show that they comply with these rules. Because non-compliance can lead to significant fines, research has focused on improving compliance verification. Current state-of-the-art largely emphasizes, for example, analyzing prescriptive models and performing post hoc log analysis to determine whether data processing conforms to GDPR. We contend that compliance can be made easier by ensuring that datasets used in processing activities are compliant with consent from the outset. This paper addresses how to generate datasets that satisfy given consent on a just-in-time basis. We propose RDF and OWL ontologies to model the consent an organization has collected and its relation to data-processing purposes. Using this ontology, we annotate schemas and generate declarative mappings that convert relational data into RDF based on those annotations. We also show how compliant datasets can be produced by modifying the mapping output. By using RDF and OWL, the entire process can be implemented declaratively with SPARQL. All components are integrated into a service that also records provenance information for each step, further increasing the transparency needed to support compliance verification. We demonstrate the approach with a synthetic dataset that simulates users giving, withdrawing, and rejecting consent for the data-processing purposes of systems. In short, the approach promotes transparency and compliance verification from the beginning, reducing the need for the post hoc compliance analysis common in current work.
